intents: real enough that you can actually see it, count it or point to it
after months of hard work you finally have results you can show people, not just hopes
the difference between a vague promise and something you could hold in your hand
ru_cue: такой, который реально можно увидеть, пощупать или измерить

upgrades.plain: After three months at the gym I finally saw [real, visible] results.
upgrades.better: After three months at the gym I finally saw *tangible* results.

upgrades.plain: My manager said that if I can't show [real] progress by Friday, the project goes to someone else.
upgrades.better: My manager said that if I can't show *tangible* progress by Friday, the project goes to someone else.

upgrades.plain: The council keeps promising 'improvements', but I want to see [real, concrete] benefits for our street, not just words.
upgrades.better: The council keeps promising 'improvements', but I want to see *tangible* benefits for our street, not just words.

nuance: About whether something is real and visible, not how big it is: a small but measurable gain is tangible; a big one is substantial.
personal: What tangible result have you seen from your English study this year?
Who do you know who prefers tangible rewards, like money, to praise?
hook: Sounds like 'танго': in a tango you hold your partner tight, solid and real in your hands.

intents: so central at a key moment that the whole outcome turns on it
describing a moment or decision that was crucial in sending your whole life in a new direction
playing the part without which the result would have been completely different
ru_cue: настолько важный, что от него зависит, куда все повернется

upgrades.plain: My chemistry teacher played a [really important] role in my decision to study medicine.
upgrades.better: My chemistry teacher played a *pivotal* role in my decision to study medicine.

upgrades.plain: That last-minute save was [what decided] the whole match.
upgrades.better: That last-minute save was *pivotal* to the whole match.

upgrades.plain: Tomorrow's interview is [hugely important] for my career, so please don't call me tonight.
upgrades.better: Tomorrow's interview is *pivotal* for my career, so please don't call me tonight.

nuance: Stronger than 'important': the outcome hinges on it. A catalyst sets change off; something pivotal is the point the whole result depends on.
personal: What was a pivotal moment in your own education?
Who played a pivotal role in making you the person you are today?
gesture: Plant one foot and swing your whole body round on it.
hook: Sounds like 'пиво-тал': the whole party turned on one thing, whether the пиво arrived.

intents: over many years, rather than right now
it costs more or hurts today, but years from now you'll be glad you did it
when you look past the short-term pain to how things finally turn out
ru_cue: если смотреть не на сегодня, а на много лет вперед

upgrades.plain: Good shoes are cheaper [over time].
upgrades.better: Good shoes are cheaper *in the long run*.

upgrades.plain: I know leaving the band hurts now, but [years from now] you'll be glad you finished your degree.
upgrades.better: I know leaving the band hurts now, but *in the long run* you'll be glad you finished your degree.

upgrades.plain: Fixing the roof properly now will save us money [later on].
upgrades.better: Fixing the roof properly now will save us money *in the long run*.

collocations.chunk: pay off in the long run
worth it in the long run

ru_trap: Russian 'в долгосрочной перспективе' tempts 'in the long perspective'; English says *in the long run* (or 'in the long term').
nuance: Weighs the later payoff against a cost now; 'eventually' only says something happens later, with no trade-off.
personal: What habit of yours will pay off in the long run?
Which friend or relative made a sacrifice that paid off in the long run?
hook: Picture a marathon: the sprinters lead at first, but the steady runner wins in the long run.

intents: make a bad situation even worse
add fuel to a problem that is already there
your attempt to deal with some trouble only makes it bigger
ru_cue: сделать и без того плохую ситуацию еще хуже

upgrades.plain: Scratching the bite will only [make the itching worse].
upgrades.better: Scratching the bite will only *exacerbate* the itching.

upgrades.plain: Mum and Dad were already arguing, and my stupid joke only [made things worse].
upgrades.better: Mum and Dad were already arguing, and my stupid joke only *exacerbated* the situation.

upgrades.plain: Cold air can [make a cough worse].
upgrades.better: Cold air can *exacerbate* a cough.

nuance: Only for something already bad: you can't exacerbate a good mood. Perpetuate keeps a problem going; exacerbate makes it worse.
personal: What tends to exacerbate your stress before an exam?
Who do you know whose 'help' usually exacerbates a problem?
hook: Sounds like 'eggs are bait': throwing eggs at a bear only makes it angrier.

intents: reduce the damage or risk that something bad will cause
you can't stop the flood, but sandbags make the damage less serious
take steps so a problem hits less hard, even though it's still there
ru_cue: уменьшить вред или риск от чего-то плохого

upgrades.plain: Sandbags [reduced] the worst of the flood damage.
upgrades.better: Sandbags *mitigated* the worst of the flood damage.

upgrades.plain: I missed the deadline, but telling my boss early helped [limit] the damage.
upgrades.better: I missed the deadline, but telling my boss early helped *mitigate* the damage.

upgrades.plain: Keeping some savings [reduces] the risk if you lose your job.
upgrades.better: Keeping some savings *mitigates* the risk if you lose your job.

nuance: For harm, risk and impact (mitigate the damage); for pain, pressure or suffering use alleviate; to stop something growing, use curb.
personal: What do you do to mitigate the stress of exam week?
Who do you know who is good at mitigating the damage after a mistake?
hook: Think 'mitt': a baseball mitt doesn't stop the hard ball, it just mitigates the damage to your hand.

intents: ease pain, suffering or pressure so someone feels better
your back aches all day, and a hot bath finally takes the edge off
ease the hardship or worry that struggling people feel, so life weighs on them less
ru_cue: облегчить боль, страдания или нагрузку

upgrades.plain: A hot bath helps [ease] the pain in my back.
upgrades.better: A hot bath helps *alleviate* the pain in my back.

upgrades.plain: When Dad was ill, my sister moving in [took a lot of the pressure off] me.
upgrades.better: When Dad was ill, my sister moving in *alleviated* a lot of the pressure on me.

upgrades.plain: A few kind words from the nurse [eased] my mum's fear before the operation.
upgrades.better: A few kind words from the nurse *alleviated* my mum's fear before the operation.

nuance: For pain, suffering, pressure, symptoms or poverty: you alleviate what people feel; you mitigate the damage or risk of an event.
personal: What alleviates your stress after a hard day?
Who has alleviated a burden for you when you really needed it?
hook: Sounds like 'all-elevate': lift all the weight off someone's shoulders, and the pain eases.

word: take it with a pinch of salt
intents: don't believe everything someone tells you; stay a little doubtful
your friend swears the fish he caught was as big as a car
listen to a claim but assume it's probably exaggerated
ru_cue: не верить до конца, слушать с долей сомнения

upgrades.plain: He says he never gets nervous, but I [don't really believe that].
upgrades.better: He says he never gets nervous, but I *take that with a pinch of salt*.

upgrades.plain: Online reviews are useful, but [don't believe everything you read].
upgrades.better: Online reviews are useful, but *take them with a pinch of salt*.

upgrades.plain: My ex told everyone the break-up was my fault, so I hope people [don't believe all of it].
upgrades.better: My ex told everyone the break-up was my fault, so I hope people *take it with a pinch of salt*.

collocations.chunk: take everything he says with a pinch of salt
I'd take those figures with a pinch of salt

nuance: Mild doubt, not rejection: you still listen, you just assume it may be exaggerated. Americans say 'a grain of salt'.
personal: What kind of advice do you always take with a pinch of salt?
Whose stories in your family do you take with a pinch of salt?
gesture: Pinch some imaginary salt and sprinkle it in the air, raising one eyebrow.
hook: A pinch of salt makes a strange dish easier to swallow, just as a little doubt makes a tall story easier to swallow.
forms: take it with a pinch of salt
takes it with a pinch of salt
took it with a pinch of salt
taken it with a pinch of salt
taking it with a pinch of salt
take that with a pinch of salt
take them with a pinch of salt
take it with a grain of salt

intents: slowly weaken someone's confidence, trust or authority
one parent says no, and the other says 'oh, go on then' right in front of the kids
eat away at the base of something until it can no longer hold up
ru_cue: постепенно ослабить чью-то уверенность, доверие или авторитет

upgrades.plain: Correcting her in front of everyone will [knock] her confidence.
upgrades.better: Correcting her in front of everyone will *undermine* her confidence.

upgrades.plain: Every time I say no, my mum says yes to the kids, and it completely [destroys] my authority.
upgrades.better: Every time I say no, my mum says yes to the kids, and it completely *undermines* my authority.

upgrades.plain: Missing deadlines [weakens] your case for promotion.
upgrades.better: Missing deadlines *undermines* your case for promotion.

nuance: Weakens something from within, often gradually or behind the scenes; the opposite of underpin. Hinder only slows progress down.
personal: Has anything ever undermined your confidence right before an exam?
Who do you know who undermines other people with 'jokes'?
gesture: Make small digging movements low down, then let your other forearm, held upright like a wall, slowly topple.
hook: under + mine: soldiers dig a tunnel under the castle wall until the whole wall collapses.

intents: be the solid base that something else rests on
the hidden support that a whole argument or relationship stands on
take this away from the bottom and everything built on top would fall apart
ru_cue: быть основой, на которой держится все остальное

upgrades.plain: Trust [is the basis of] every good friendship.
upgrades.better: Trust *underpins* every good friendship.

upgrades.plain: Careful research [supports] her whole argument.
upgrades.better: Careful research *underpins* her whole argument.

upgrades.plain: After he lied about the money, I realised honesty [was what our whole marriage rested on].
upgrades.better: After he lied about the money, I realised honesty *underpinned* our whole marriage.

nuance: About foundations: it holds something up from below (the opposite of undermine). Foster helps something grow; underpin keeps it standing.
personal: What value underpins the way you make big decisions?
What do you think underpins your best friend's success?
hook: under + pin: a steel pin under the shelf holds the whole thing up.

intents: make it easier for something to happen or for people to do something, by helping rather than doing it yourself
guide a group discussion along without taking sides yourself
be the helpful go-between who makes it easier for a meeting, a deal or learning to take place
ru_cue: сделать так, чтобы процесс шел легче и глаже

upgrades.plain: The new app [makes it easier to book] a doctor's appointment.
upgrades.better: The new app *facilitates* booking a doctor's appointment.

upgrades.plain: A neutral person can [help run] a difficult discussion.
upgrades.better: A neutral person can *facilitate* a difficult discussion.

upgrades.plain: My boss asked me to [run] the workshop tomorrow, and I'm terrified.
upgrades.better: My boss asked me to *facilitate* the workshop tomorrow, and I'm terrified.

ru_trap: Russian 'способствовать чему-то' tempts 'facilitate to something'; English takes a direct object: facilitate the process.
nuance: For processes and actions (booking, trade, a discussion); foster is for feelings and qualities that grow over time.
personal: What tool or habit facilitates your studying the most?
Who do you know who is good at facilitating a tense meeting?
hook: Sounds like French 'facile' (easy): to facilitate is to make it facile.

intents: get in the way and slow down progress
heavy snow means the rescue team takes twice as long to reach people
make it harder for someone to move forward, without stopping them completely
ru_cue: мешать двигаться вперед, тормозить

upgrades.plain: Heavy snow [slowed down] the rescue.
upgrades.better: Heavy snow *hindered* the rescue.

upgrades.plain: Too many meetings [get in the way of] actual work.
upgrades.better: Too many meetings *hinder* actual work.

upgrades.plain: I didn't get the job; I think my nerves [held me back] in the interview.
upgrades.better: I didn't get the job; I think my nerves *hindered* me in the interview.

nuance: Slows or blocks progress; it doesn't weaken the thing itself (undermine) or make a problem worse (exacerbate).
personal: What hinders your progress most when you study?
Who do you know whose plans were hindered by a lack of money or time?
gesture: Hold one arm out stiffly in front of you, as if blocking someone trying to walk past.
hook: Sounds like 'hind leg': a dog hanging on to your hind leg hinders every step you take.

intents: do more than anyone expects or requires of you
a shop assistant drives your forgotten bag to your house after closing time
put in more effort than the job needs, just to do it really well for someone
ru_cue: сделать больше, чем от тебя требуется
plain: do more than you have to

upgrades.plain: She always [does more than she has to] for her students.
upgrades.better: She always *goes the extra mile* for her students.

upgrades.plain: The hotel lost our booking, but they [really made an effort] and upgraded us for free.
upgrades.better: The hotel lost our booking, but they *went the extra mile* and upgraded us for free.

upgrades.plain: If you want this job, you'll have to [do more than everyone else].
upgrades.better: If you want this job, you'll have to *go the extra mile*.

collocations.chunk: willing to go the extra mile
go the extra mile for customers

nuance: Praises effort beyond duty, usually to help someone; it's about doing more, not about being careful (meticulous).
personal: When did you last go the extra mile at work or school?
Which teacher or colleague always goes the extra mile?
hook: Picture a runner who finishes the race, then jogs one more mile to carry a stranger's bag home.

intents: keep a bad habit or a growing problem under control
your spending on takeaways is getting out of hand, so you set yourself a limit
hold back an urge or a temper, like pulling on a horse's reins
ru_cue: держать в рамках и не давать разрастись чему-то вредному

upgrades.plain: I'm trying to [control] my spending on takeaways.
upgrades.better: I'm trying to *curb* my spending on takeaways.

upgrades.plain: He nearly lost his job for shouting at a client, so now he's learning to [control] his temper.
upgrades.better: He nearly lost his job for shouting at a client, so now he's learning to *curb* his temper.

upgrades.plain: The council brought in parking charges to [cut down] traffic in the centre.
upgrades.better: The council brought in parking charges to *curb* traffic in the centre.

nuance: Restrains something that tends to grow (spending, a temper, traffic); mitigate softens damage, deter stops people before they start.
personal: What habit would you most like to curb?
Who do you know who managed to curb a bad habit, and how?
gesture: Pull both fists back towards your chest, like tightening a horse's reins.
hook: Sounds like 'kerb', the edge of the pavement that stops a car from going too far.

intents: help a feeling, skill or relationship grow slowly over time
a teacher builds the kind of classroom where shy kids start to speak up
create the conditions in which something good, like trust or talent, can develop
ru_cue: создавать условия, в которых постепенно растет что-то хорошее

upgrades.plain: Eating together every evening [helps build] a closer family.
upgrades.better: Eating together every evening *fosters* a closer family.

upgrades.plain: Small classes [encourage] real discussion.
upgrades.better: Small classes *foster* real discussion.

upgrades.plain: When the other teachers had given up on me, one patient tutor [built up] my confidence.
upgrades.better: When the other teachers had given up on me, one patient tutor *fostered* my confidence.

nuance: For feelings, skills and relationships that grow slowly; facilitate makes a process easier. A 'foster family' raises someone else's child.
personal: What fostered your interest in English?
Who fostered your confidence when you were younger?
hook: Think of a foster parent: someone who takes in a child and helps it grow, day by day.

intents: decide how much money, time or space goes to each purpose
splitting the family budget: this much for rent, this much for food, this much for fun
hand out a fixed amount of something to particular people or tasks
ru_cue: решить, сколько денег, времени или места отдать на каждую цель

upgrades.plain: The council will [give out] the money next month.
upgrades.better: The council will *allocate* the money next month.

upgrades.plain: We [set aside] an hour every evening for homework.
upgrades.better: We *allocate* an hour every evening to homework.

upgrades.plain: We didn't [leave] enough time for testing, and the app crashed in front of the client.
upgrades.better: We didn't *allocate* enough time for testing, and the app crashed in front of the client.

ru_trap: Russian 'выделить время на что-то' tempts 'allocate time on'; English says allocate time *to* or *for* something.
nuance: About dividing up a limited amount among purposes; prioritise only decides what comes first, not how much each thing gets.
personal: How much time do you allocate to English each week?
Who in your family decides how the money is allocated?
hook: Sounds like 'a lot o' cake': you allocate the cake, one slice to each guest.

intents: actually put a plan or decision into practice
the plan was agreed months ago, and now someone has to make it really happen
the hard part after deciding: making new rules or a new system work in real life
ru_cue: воплотить принятый план или решение в жизнь

upgrades.plain: Planning a new diet is easy; the hard part is [actually putting it into practice].
upgrades.better: Planning a new diet is easy; the hard part is *implementing* it.

upgrades.plain: The school [brought in] a new marking scheme.
upgrades.better: The school *implemented* a new marking scheme.

upgrades.plain: If we don't [carry out] the new safety rules properly, someone is going to get hurt.
upgrades.better: If we don't *implement* the new safety rules properly, someone is going to get hurt.

ru_trap: Russian 'реализовать план' tempts 'realise a plan'; English says *implement* a plan ('realise' means understand).
nuance: The doing after a decision (policies, systems, changes); advocate argues for a plan, facilitate makes it easier.
personal: What change have you planned but never actually implemented?
Has a manager or teacher you know ever implemented a rule that everyone hated?
hook: Sounds like 'имплант': the dentist doesn't just plan it, he actually puts it in.

word: hit the nail on the head
intents: say exactly what the real issue is
a friend sums up in one sentence what you've been trying to explain for an hour
find the perfectly accurate words for what's really going on
ru_cue: точно назвать самую суть дела

upgrades.plain: You're [exactly right]: it's not the money, it's the hours.
upgrades.better: You've *hit the nail on the head*: it's not the money, it's the hours.

upgrades.plain: When Mum said I was only angry because I was homesick, she [was completely right], and I burst into tears.
upgrades.better: When Mum said I was only angry because I was homesick, she *hit the nail on the head*, and I burst into tears.

upgrades.plain: That question [got right to the real point].
upgrades.better: That question *hit the nail on the head*.

collocations.chunk: you've hit the nail on the head
really hit the nail on the head

nuance: Praises an accurate remark or diagnosis; it's about saying the right thing, not about agreeing (that's being on the same page).
personal: When did someone hit the nail on the head about a problem of yours?
Who in your family usually hits the nail on the head about other people?
gesture: Bring an imaginary hammer down in one clean, precise strike.
hook: One clean hammer blow right on the nail's head: no bent nail, no sore thumb, like 'попасть в точку'.
forms: hit the nail on the head
hits the nail on the head
hitting the nail on the head

intents: decide what matters most and deal with that first
with exams next week, studying comes before going out
put your tasks in order of importance when you can't do everything
ru_cue: решить, что важнее всего, и заняться этим в первую очередь

upgrades.plain: With exams next week, I need to [put studying before] going out.
upgrades.better: With exams next week, I need to *prioritise* studying over going out.

upgrades.plain: At A&E they [deal first with] the most urgent cases.
upgrades.better: At A&E they *prioritise* the most urgent cases.

upgrades.plain: I said yes to everything and missed my daughter's school play; I really need to learn to [decide what matters most].
upgrades.better: I said yes to everything and missed my daughter's school play; I really need to learn to *prioritise*.

ru_trap: Russian 'расставить приоритеты' tempts 'place priorities'; English says 'set priorities', or simply *prioritise*.
nuance: Decides the order (what comes first); allocate divides up how much time or money each thing gets.
personal: What do you prioritise on a busy weekday morning?
Who do you know who always prioritises family over work?
hook: 'Prior' means 'before': the most important job goes before all the rest.

intents: speak out publicly in favour of an idea or a change
a doctor who keeps telling everyone to walk thirty minutes a day
argue for a cause and try to win other people over to it
ru_cue: открыто выступать за какую-то идею и убеждать в ней других

upgrades.plain: My doctor [recommends] walking for thirty minutes a day.
upgrades.better: My doctor *advocates* walking for thirty minutes a day.

upgrades.plain: She has long [argued for] shorter working weeks.
upgrades.better: She has long *advocated* shorter working weeks.

upgrades.plain: At the family meeting I was the only one who [spoke up for] selling the house, and everyone glared at me.
upgrades.better: At the family meeting I was the only one who *advocated* selling the house, and everyone glared at me.

ru_trap: Russian 'адвокат' suggests a court lawyer; the English verb just means to argue publicly for an idea, no court involved.
nuance: More active and public than 'support'. The verb ends in /eɪt/; the noun (an advocate, a supporter) ends in /ət/.
personal: What change in education would you advocate?
Who do you know who advocates a healthy lifestyle a little too loudly?
hook: Sounds like 'адвокат': a lawyer stands up and argues for his client, just as you advocate an idea.

intents: say what caused something, or who deserves the credit for it
your grandmother says her long life is all thanks to her daily walk
explain a result by naming the reason behind it
ru_cue: сказать, что причина чего-то именно в этом

upgrades.plain: She says her good health [is thanks to] swimming every morning.
upgrades.better: She *attributes* her good health to swimming every morning.

upgrades.plain: The delay was [put down to] bad weather.
upgrades.better: The delay was *attributed* to bad weather.

upgrades.plain: I failed my driving test, and I [blame it on] nerves, not bad driving!
upgrades.better: I failed my driving test, and I *attribute* it to nerves, not bad driving!

collocations.frame: the delay can be ___ to bad weather

ru_trap: Russian 'объяснять чем-то' tempts 'attribute by' or 'attribute with'; English always says attribute X *to* Y.
nuance: Names a cause or source, neutrally, unlike 'blame'. The noun (AT-tribute) means a quality and is stressed on the first syllable.
personal: What do you attribute your progress in English to?
To what does someone in your family attribute their success?
hook: Sounds like 'a tribute': at the awards, the winner pays a tribute to her coach and attributes the win to him.

intents: be the perfect, typical case of a quality or style
your grandmother, who feeds every visitor, is the perfect example of what kindness looks like
if someone asks what this style looks like, you just point to this one building
ru_cue: быть типичным или образцовым воплощением чего-то

upgrades.plain: That building [is a perfect example of] the style of the period.
upgrades.better: That building *exemplifies* the style of the period.

upgrades.plain: Her career [shows] what hard work can do.
upgrades.better: Her career *exemplifies* what hard work can do.

upgrades.plain: My boss lost the file and blamed me; it [sums up] everything that's wrong with that office.
upgrades.better: My boss lost the file and blamed me; it *exemplifies* everything that's wrong with that office.

nuance: The thing itself is the model case (she exemplifies kindness); a speaker gives an example, the example exemplifies.
personal: What habit of yours exemplifies your personality?
Who do you know who exemplifies patience?
hook: Sounds like 'экземпляр': this one copy shows exactly what all the others are like.

intents: suddenly, with no warning and no reason you could see
an old friend you haven't heard from in ten years rings you on a random Tuesday
happening from nowhere, at the moment you least expect it
ru_cue: совершенно неожиданно, словно из ниоткуда

upgrades.plain: She called me [unexpectedly] after ten years.
upgrades.better: She called me *out of the blue* after ten years.

upgrades.plain: [Completely without warning], my boss told me I was being let go.
upgrades.better: *Out of the blue*, my boss told me I was being let go.

upgrades.plain: The job offer came [from nowhere].
upgrades.better: The job offer came *out of the blue*.

collocations.chunk: rang me completely out of the blue
collocations.frame: she rang me completely ___ after ten years

collocations.chunk: called me out of the blue

nuance: About surprise timing with no warning; unprecedented means it has never happened before, not that it was unexpected.
personal: What is the most surprising thing that has happened to you out of the blue?
Who has got in touch with you out of the blue after a long time?
hook: A clear blue sky, then a bolt of lightning from nowhere: 'как гром среди ясного неба'.
